item.content:encoded:
The Wild Card series against the Yankees was probably the worst way for the 2026 season to end. Everything that was a problem at any point - struggles to score runs, the bullpen, injuries - all happened at the same time and within a matter of minutes. Two games in a row ended the Red Sox season. This wasn’t the plan. As all the Sox players returned from the WBC to Fort Myers, many riding hot streaks, this looked like a team ready to rocket. Yes, there were questions entering the season. But there were answers that hadn’t been fully formed yet.
After the 2025 season, the Sox were desperate for infield help. Trevor Story, not a guarantee of health or success himself, since arriving in Boston, was coming off a tremendous year, his best for the Red Sox. The rest of the infield was a question mark. Third base was more-or-less vacant after Alex Bregman opted out. Second base was going to be a battle with the future potential of Marcelo Mayer as a leading contestant. First base? Triston Casas? Maybe? Catcher, using the more generous definition of infield, was a tandem based on Carlos Narváez hitting in 2025 and Connor Wong, who couldn’t hit at all. There were at least two guys, which was more than could be said about first base.
Craig Breslow looked at the free agent market. He looked at the trade market. He looked at his own farm system. And in two phases he built the roster that he would live or die with.
We know about phase one. Caleb Durbin was acquired from the Milwaukee Brewers. Willson Contreras was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals. Isaiah Kiner-Falefa was signed to platoon (kinda) with Mayer.
On the free agent market, the Red Sox went in the opposite direction. The promise/hope was two bats. And they passed on Pete Alonso, Alex Bregman, Bo Bichette etc. Aside from Contreras there were no big bats.
What Durbin would share with Willson, besides become Mini Bowser to his Bowser, was control. Contreras was guaranteed to be in town through 2027 with an option for 2028. Durbin will not hit free agency until the 2030s. The same with Mayer. Ranger Suarez, on the other side of the ball, also was signed long-term.
As it would turn out Willson Contreras would not even sniff competition from Triston Casas, who would face a series of injuries that would cost him the season. Not that anyone was worried about having too many first basemen. Caleb Durbin would start off slow with the bat, glacial even, but provide solid defense. He’d go on to set a new career high in home runs while, likely, competing for a Gold Glove.
Marcelo Mayer would underperform and then get hurt. Carlos Narváez would revert to his reputation as a bat-second player. While Connor Wong would provide some offense in a bounce-back season, the catcher tandem as a whole was underwater.
Phase two would be at the deadline. With Durbin rounding into form as The Durbinator, Breslow and his team set their sights on second base and catcher. Turning Connelly Early into Curtis Mead gave them another second baseman with control for years to come. And while the sample size is small, Mead hit 17 home runs in just 87 games. Adding a 30-homer threat to second base would be a tremendous pillar of the offense. Mayer would be traded separately, Mead would get hurt, but the plan was in place.
Similarly, the massive all-in prospect trade for Adley Rutschman was for 2026 and 2027. Connor Wong isn’t a free agent until after the 2028 season so catcher is set for another year and they have time to evaluate Rutschman or find a replacement before 2028. For Breslow’s plan through this summer, when he didn’t know he’d be extended, that’s all that mattered. Build then best team for what could be his last season if they struggled.
Entering 2027 the Red Sox have two catchers. They have an entire starting infield, plus top prospect Franklin Arias. They have Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Wilyer Abreu (plus control of Jarren Duran, and Masataka Yoshida, and Kristian Campbell) in the outfield.
The rotation has Payton Tolle, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, and Jake Bennett. Boston holds an option on Sonny Gray that he can opt out of, but potentially the entire rotation is headed back for 2027. Starters 6-10 might be a concern, but for a healthy Opening Day major league roster, Breslow took care of that already.
We never actually got to see this team assembled together in 2026. Even if Curtis Mead came into the last game of the season while Garrett Crochet was on the mound, Roman was out. This year, unless there is a big trade to accommodate a move, the Hot Stove season won’t be the same. The roster is basically set. Did Breslow see the lockout as an obstacle? Maybe! He might have been thinking that teams would scramble to make moves before and after and he’d be set. For a team that was seeing it’s window open in 2025, it seems too intentional to put together the whole thing one year in with really only the Story to Arias transition as a big roster move to facilitate.
The performance of the team in 2026 was up and down, but overall we saw a number of good years from this group - Tolle, Abreu, Contreras, Rafaela, and Durbin all provide reasons to be optimistic. Roman Anthony had a good run around the hand injury. Six months off sure would be nice to let that heal. There’s reason to think 2027 can be fun. Maybe distributed a little better too.
Your Opening Day 2027 Boston Red Sox:
C: Rutschman, Wong
1: Contreras
2B: Mead, Sogard
SS: Story, Arias
3B: Durbin
OF: Roman, Rafaela, Abreau, Duran (if he’s not moved/non-tenderd), Campbell
DH: Yoshida

ア・リーグ、ワイルドカードシリーズ第2戦（ヤンキース9−2レッドソックス、30日、ニューヨーク）米大リーグ、レッドソックスはライバル地のニューヨークで本領を発揮できず、連敗を喫しワイルドカードシリーズでの敗退が決まった。吉田正尚外野手（33）はシーズン終盤に左太もも裏の負傷でワイルドカードシリーズのメンバーから外れ、終戦を見守った。
「一言で言えば、みんなが失望している。それだけは間違いない。素晴らしい選手たちだし、このグループのことが大好き。ワールドシリーズを制することが目標だった。それが今夜、僕たちにとって終わってしまった、とても悔しい」
トレーシー監督は試合後肩を落として心境を語った。前日完封負けして後がないチームは36歳ベテラングレイが先発。三回までは無失点でリズムよく試合を運んだが、四回先頭のガルシアに内角低めのスイーパーを捉えられ右中間に先制ソロを献上。五回も先頭から安打を許し、2死一、三塁の場面で交代となった。2番手に上がったミラーも2番ベリンジャーに右前適時打を許すと、3番手には左肩を痛め今季ほぼ全休だった先発クロシェがマウンドへ。昨季18勝を挙げ流れを変えたい左腕だったが3者連続安打や味方の失策も重なり1死も奪えず4失点でノックアウト。4番手のウィットロックもベリンジャーに3ランを浴びるなど強豪打線を抑え切れなかった。さらに打線は前日の3安打完封負けに続きこの日もわずか4安打2得点と振わず。悔いが残る終戦となった。
チームは今年4月前任のコーラ氏がチーム低迷で解任され、3Aウースターを率いていたトレーシー監督が昇格。地区最下位だったチームを立て直し、2連続プレーオフ進出に導いていた。既に29年までの契約が決まっているトレーシー監督は指揮1年目を問われると「今この瞬間の正直な答えとしては、そんなことは考えていない。いろいろなことがあった1年だったのは確かだけど、今は何よりも、プレーオフのシリーズで負けたという事実しか考えられない」とまだ現実を受け入れられない様子だった。

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The news worsened for Red Sox outfielder/designated hitter Roman Anthony on Wednesday when he was taken off the roster for the remainder of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees after imaging back in Boston showed additional strains in his right wrist.
The fact that Anthony was taken off the Wild Card Series roster means he would be ineligible to play in the AL Division Series against the Rays, should Boston advance.
“I feel sick to my stomach. I haven't slept much,” said Anthony. “It doesn't really feel real, to be honest. There's so many different emotions and feelings throughout the course of this rehab process this year that to kind of get to this same news again, and even worse, it's just like, I don't know. It's hard to have an answer to anything right now.”
Mead has turned a corner of late with his hitting progression, recently taking live batting practice. His ramp-up to postseason action was accelerated due to Anthony’s injury, and several others (Mickey Gasper, Masataka Yoshida and Romy Gonzalez) also being unavailable due to health reasons.
“There are times when you accelerate timelines and compress things,” said Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. “You still want to make sure you have the interests of the player and the team in mind. We’re not going to do anything that’s reckless or irresponsible, but medically, Curtis is cleared.”
Losing Anthony was tough timing for the Red Sox, who took a 9-0 loss in Game 1 of this best-of-three series. Sensing immediately it was more than a minor setback, the team hired a car to drive Anthony back to Boston after the game, and he had imaging taken on Wednesday morning.
“He is sore,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “He was sent back last night after leaving the game. Sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging, which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist, in addition to exacerbating the old [finger] injury. So it's not great.”
The sensation Anthony felt in his at-bats in Game 1 was familiar in a nauseating way.
“Basically the same thing that happened early on in the year in addition to other strains in a few muscles in other areas in the hand. So, to shorten it up, it's the same thing with more added on,” said Anthony. “Yeah. It’s brutal. It’s confusing. There’s a lot of different emotions going on that I don’t know. It’s tough to put into words, and I feel like I grinded all year throughout something to get to where I am right now and to get to play in a game last night. And for that to happen, it’s confusing and it sucks.”
The Red Sox were equally confused by the recurrence.
“As far as I know, the rehab and the return to play was the appropriate one,” said Breslow. “Last night in the game, he did something where things changed, things worsened and we need to take a fresh look at it.”
Other than feeling occasional “zingers” on swings since his return to action on Aug. 30, Anthony hadn’t felt anything close to the discomfort that took place in Game 1, when he exited the game in the sixth inning after striking out in his first two at-bats.
The best-case scenario is that rest and rehab help Anthony recover, and that surgery won’t be necessary.
“I think we're still trying to figure out exactly what happened and what the prognosis will be,” said Breslow. “It’s still so recent that we’re collecting information, and I'm sure we'll examine all of those things.”
The 22-year-old left-handed hitter has had mixed results since returning to action, slashing .262/.321/.476 with four homers and 10 RBIs in his final 103 regular-season at-bats.
“I’ve been experiencing some things with the swings and check swings over the past six weeks, and last night just felt a little more intense than past swings have and lingered a little bit longer than the ones that I had before, so it was super alarming,” Anthony said. “It got to a point where it was tough to grip a bat, so I knew this was similar to the one earlier on in the year, and that’s why we decided to go get imaging.”
And now, the Red Sox will try to win without Anthony, which they did earlier in the season, most notably during that 32-5 stretch from June 25-Aug. 8. For that to happen, players will have to heat up. Boston’s offense has been cold as a unit for weeks.
“I think he's a special talent. He's a special guy,” said Breslow. “Right now we're focused on making sure that we put ourselves in a position to win the game tonight and figure out everything that's going on with Roman's wrist. I think to talk beyond that is probably foolish at this point.”

Lost amid the embarrassing madness of Tuesday's Wild Card series opener between the Boston Red Sox and the New York Yankees was Roman Anthony being pinch-hit for midway through the game, seemingly out of nowhere. After the game, it was revealed by manager Chad Tracy that Anthony had re-aggravated the wrist injury that had kept him out for more than three months during the regular season — and that his Game 2 status was up in the air.
Well, Boston's Game 2 lineup is out, and it's safe to say the fan base won't like it, with Anthony on the bench.
Is Roman Anthony playing tonight? Red Sox's lineup gives answer
Here's a look at Boston's Anthony-less lineup against Yankees left-hander Max Fried.
| Player | Position |
|---|---|
| 1. Jahmai Jones | DH |
| 2. Adley Rutschman | C |
| 3. Willson Contreras | 1B |
| 4. Wilyer Abreu | RF |
| 5. Ceddanne Rafaela | CF |
| 6. Caleb Durbin | 3B |
| 7. Nick Sogard | 2B |
| 8. Trevor Story | SS |
| 9. Nate Eaton | LF |
Yeah, the Red Sox are going to miss Anthony dearly. Sure, there's the makings of a decent lineup here. Jahmai Jones has done nothing but crush lefties since the Red Sox acquired him. Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras are proven stars. Wilyer Abreu has broken out against left-handers this season, in particular. Ceddanne Rafaela is having his best offensive year. Still, there's no replacing Anthony.
He only appeared in 55 regular-season games and didn't look great in his two at-bats on Tuesday, but nobody in Boston's organization has a higher ceiling than Anthony. Being without him makes the already daunting challenge of rebounding from an 0-1 deficit in the best-of-three series that much more difficult.
Red Sox's growing injury report makes it tougher to believe in dream run
What makes Anthony's injury that much more difficult is that he's far from the only one. The Red Sox have a slew of notables on the IL, and that's making achieving their ultimate gol tough to believe in.
| Player | Position | Injury | Return |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mickey Gasper | C/INF | Right biceps strain | 2027 |
| Tyron Guerrero | RHP | Right shoulder strain | 2027 |
| Eli White | INF/OF | Ligament damage in right foot | 2027 |
| Curtis Mead | INF | Left wrist fracture | Postseason or 2027 |
| Kutter Crawford | RHP | Right flexor irritation | 2027 |
| Johan Oviedo | RHP | Right flexor strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Anthony Siegler | INF | Right wrist discomfort | Postseason or 2027 |
| Justin Slaten | RHP | Right elbow inflammation | 2027 |
| Masataka Yoshida | DH | Left hamstring strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Triston Casas | 1B | Left abdominal strain | 2027 |
The list is lengthy and littered with quality talent. Lineup-wise, the Red Sox sure could use Mickey Gasper, who was one of their hottest hitters before suffering his injury, right about now. They could also use Curtis Mead, a player who crushes left-handed pitching. Even Masataka Yoshida's bat would really come in handy with Anthony out.
Pitching-wise, Boston's depth has taken a hit. Tyron Guerrero and Justin Slaten are two of the most important members of their bullpen, and perhaps they would've been able to keep the game closer on Tuesday had they been healthy. Guys like Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo are proven back-end starters who could've eaten innings this October.
Perhaps the Red Sox can get Mead and a few others back if they can get past the Yankees, but with Anthony now joining the laundry list of injured players, it's getting tough to believe in them making a comeback.

Mickey Gasper’s stunning breakout season with the Boston Red Sox ended in an instant Friday, when a two-strike swing tore his right biceps clean off the bone, according to a report by Red Sox WEEI reporter Rob Bradford.
Boston will play its wild-card playoff series, and any other playoff series should they advance, without the utility man whose midsummer power binge turned into one of the best stories of the club’s late-season turnaround, leaving manager Chad Tracy’s bench thinned out at the worst possible time.
Gasper was catching Game 1 of Friday’s doubleheader against the Chicago Cubs at Fenway Park when he swung through a fifth-inning strikeout and immediately grabbed at his arm. He grimaced walking back to the dugout, and Connor Wong took over behind the plate before the top of the sixth.
How Mickey Gasper’s Boston Red Sox Injury Happened
“At this point, it looks like a significant biceps injury, so he’s going to still be seeing more doctors and stuff like that,” Tracy said, as quoted by MLB.com‘s Ian Browne. “We’ll get the final conclusion, but it’s a pretty significant biceps injury. It’s probably going to take him out.”
That turned out to be an understatement. According to Bradford, Gasper will return to Boston where he will have surgery on his right biceps on Friday.
Sports medicine physician Jesse Morse described a full-thickness tear of the tendon, meaning the biceps separated entirely from the bone and surgery is the only fix. Morse said recovery typically runs six to eight weeks with no expected long-term effect, putting Gasper on track to be ready for offseason work and spring training in 2027.
The Red Sox placed Gasper on the 10-day injured list Sunday, retroactive to Sept. 26, with a right biceps strain. As a result, Gasper was left off the Red Sox playoff roster, but worse than that, the 30-year-old from New Hampshire‘s season, and any hope of playing in the postseason, is over.
Gasper’s bat against right-handers had turned into a real option against playoff pitching. Now Boston enters October counting on Jarren Duran and Roman Anthony to cover left field and DH against right-handers, with one fewer safety net.
Mickey Gasper’s Breakout and Long Road to Boston
Gasper made his major league debut in August 2024, and proceeded to go 0-for-18 in his brief call-up.
Gasper hit just .243 in his first big league stint of this year before Boston optioned him back to Triple-A Worcester in late June. Recalled Aug. 16 after Masataka Yoshida’s injury, he turned into a different hitter almost overnight, running a scorching stretch that produced the second-highest monthly OPS by any hitter with at least 40 plate appearances in a single month, trailing only Barry Bonds’ otherworldly April of 2004.
He backed it up with a seven-game run that ranked sixth all time in OPS, behind only Bonds, Shawn Green, Bryce Harper, Babe Ruth and Josh Hamilton. He finished the year having hit 10 homers with 24 RBI in 67 games, splitting time at catcher, first base and designated hitter.
The switch-hitter’s path to Fenway Park ran through eight minor league seasons. The Yankees took him in the 27th round of the 2018 draft out of Bryant University, where he became the first position player from the program to reach the majors, joining pitchers Keith MacWhorter and James Karinchak, his old college roommate. He debuted with Boston in 2024, went to Minnesota that winter in a trade, bounced through Washington on waivers, landing back with the Red Sox to start 2026.
Gasper is expected to be back in the mix for a utility role next season. For now, the Red Sox move forward into the playoffs without the unlikeliest hitter of their season.

item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.

Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

The Boston Red Sox are just a few days away from kicking off a three-game wild-card series against the New York Yankees on the road for the second straight season.
Boston and New York will begin the postseason run on Sep. 29. As the regular season has wrapped up, the biggest red flag for the Red Sox has been their sluggish offense. Throughout the month of September, Boston's offense has been one of the worst in the league. In fact, Boston has scored the fewest runs in baseball in September with just 69 in 23 games. But there is a bright spot, Boston fans. Roman Anthony is starting to look like himself at the plate at the perfect time.
Since Sep. 18, Anthony has batted .357 (10-for-28) with one homer, four doubles and a triple in seven games played. That's the type of production that is going to get the offense back on track. With Willson Contreras up in the air with his hand sore after getting hit by a pitch and Mickey Gasper also getting hurt, Boston needs guys to step up right now. The lights are starting to get bright. Boston has just one more regular season game left on Sunday before the full focus will turn to the playoffs.
Roman Anthony Is Getting Hot
If the Red Sox are going to make a run, they're going to need a lot from Anthony. When healthy, the Red Sox have arguably the deepest lineup in the American League playoffs, but will they actually find a way to get healthy? That's the question. Again, Contreras is up in the air. Gasper hurt his bicep on Friday and the club didn't give an optimistic update in the aftermath. Curtis Mead is on the shelf right now, although he is working his way back. Ceddanne Rafaela missed some time. Masataka Yoshida is on the Injured List as well, and the list goes on and on.
Boston isn't entering the playoffs at full strength, so it needs the guys who are healthy to carry the load to give this club enough time to advance and get closer to full strength. There isn't a guy in the lineup who moves the needle more than Anthony when he's rolling. We've started to see signs of that. If you have Anthony consistently getting on base at the top of the order, there's still enough talent behind him to get some runs in.
Boston's biggest strength is the pitching. The rotation and bullpen have carried the load all season. If they keep pitching as they have, Boston won't need many runs to win games. If Anthony can keep up his recent hot streak, that could be enough to help push Boston forward. He's that impactful.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras remained absent from the Red Sox’ lineup Thursday night at Fenway Park, seven days after he got hit by a pitch and bruised his right hand.
Is it fair to say he will be ready for the start of the playoffs?
“I hope so,” manager Chad Tracy said before the team’s finale with the Guardians. “I hope so. But [the Red Sox] want to see how he gets through all this stuff and where he’s at. And my hope is — at least for now — that he swings and feels even better than he did the other day, and then we’ll go from there.”
The first baseman took batting practice in the indoor cage, as he did earlier in the week.
It would be “huge,” Tracy said, if he was ready in time to play at any point during the Cubs series. Otherwise, he may well roll into the AL Wild Card Series without having faced live pitching in nearly two weeks.
“But I also think you’re talking about a guy [who has] a pretty good idea of his swing,” Tracy said. “[With] Willson not being down that long, the most important thing is that he’s healthy. So if he’s healthy and feeling good about it, where we’re able to get him some at-bats, that’d be great. But we’re still going to be reactive to how he’s feeling.”
Weather watch
The Cubs-Red Sox series remains in flux.
They will attempt to play a doubleheader at Fenway Park on Friday, with 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. first pitches, before a potential nor’easter arrives.
Yet to be decided: where and when the teams play their regular-season finale. Although it is scheduled for 7:15 p.m. Saturday in Boston, it could be moved to another venue, such as Tampa Bay, if the weekend forecast remains horrendous.
If the game is moved, the clubs would leave Friday night and likely play at 3 p.m. Sunday, same as all of the other finales.
MLB and the teams intend to make a call by midday Friday about what to do about Game 162.
“In a nutshell, it doesn’t look good. That’s basically what I’ve heard,” Tracy said of the weather. “Seems like we should be able to get that [doubleheader] in even [if during] the second game there might be a little bit of drizzle or whatever. It doesn’t look bad, at least what I’m seeing, and then figure out what happens next.”
Crochet on the move
A wrinkle from the weather: Garrett Crochet (left shoulder injury) will head to Fort Myers, Fla., on Friday so that he can throw an inning of live batting practice on Saturday.
The Sox have a stash of Triple-A hitters, including infielders Romy Gonzalez and Franklin Arias, working out at Fenway South.
Rafaela OK
Ceddanne Rafaela turned out to be just fine after a scare Wednesday.
The Thursday MRI on his right hamstring came back “clean,” Tracy said, affirming Rafaela’s stance from the night prior that his exit after two innings was no big deal.
“The feel is that it was a cramp, probably actually precipitated by the diving catch an inning prior],” Tracy said. “He tends to dive, and he does have low back/hip stuff that throws him out of the line for a second, that’ll manifest itself in feeling [the hamstring].”
Rafaela was back in the lineup against the Guardians, batting sixth and playing center field. It was his second game back from a right quad strain.
Major honors from minors
The Red Sox announced their annual minor league award winners, a group headed by Arias, the offensive player of the year. He slashed .323/.400/.557 with 25 homers and 91 RBIs in 117 games with Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, emerging as one of the top prospects in all of the minors.
Lefthander Dylan Brown was named pitcher of the year. A 22-year-old starter, he had a 3.46 ERA and 143 strikeouts in 106⅔ innings with Low-A Salem and High-A Greenville.
Other honored were catcher Gerardo Rodriguez (defensive player of the year), outfielder Andrews Opata (baserunner of the year), outfielder Joskairo Ramirez (Latin program position player of the year), and righthander Emanuel Jimenez (Latin program pitcher of the year).
Mead update
Infielder Curtis Mead (left wrist fracture) plans to take another step forward Friday by taking batting practice off of a machine. He will head to Fort Myers with Crochet and potentially hit against him on Saturday, he said. He is not ruled out for the first round of the playoffs beginning Tuesday, but that deadline might be too soon … Tracy left Roman Anthony out of the lineup to give him a day off. The outfielder had started 22 consecutive games since returning from the IL, batting .242 with a .726 OPS … Eli White was back at Fenway for the first time since season-ending right foot surgery Tuesday. He said he is due for a three-month recovery. That timeline would allow the outfielder to get almost all the way back to full health before the expected lockout on Dec. 1, at which point teams will not be allowed to communicate with players … Infielder Anthony Seigler said he was diagnosed with a carpal boss, a bony lump on the back of his right hand/wrist — the same injury that plagued catcher Connor Wong last year. Wong wound up having surgery to get it removed. Seigler said he has not discussed that possibility with the Red Sox … DH/outfielder Masataka Yoshida (left hamstring strain) appeared on the field at Fenway, playing catch and doing light agility drills … Dustin Pedroia and his family, in town this week, were on the field about five hours before first pitch against Cleveland, chatting with Red Sox personnel. His three sons made sure to poke their head into the Green Monster.

item.content:encoded:
レッドソックスの吉田正尚外野手（３３）が厳しい状況を迎えている。現在も左足ハムストリングの負傷で故障者リスト入りしており、ポストシーズンのロースター入りも望み薄。ＭＬＢ４年目の今季もケガに悩まされて８７試合で打率２割７分４厘、５本塁打、２８打点にとどまり、結果を出せなかった。吉田をめぐっては何度となく放出の噂があったが、そのたびに５年９０００万ドル（約１４２億円）の高額契約が足かせとなって移籍には至らなかったとされる。
しかし、今シーズンも期待を裏切り、契約期間が来年まで続くことを思えば球団の我慢も限界。米メディア「アルバット」は「吉田はまさに時限爆弾だ。かつてフロントの最も大胆な賭けの１つと見られたこの日本人スターは度重なるケガとその真の実力に対する疑問に悩まされてきた。彼は現在も故障者リスト入りし、プレーオフのロースター入りも疑問符だ」と切り捨てている。
さらに「２０２７年まで年俸１８００万ドル（約２８億円）を受け取る彼は、長打力も守備力もない指名打者だ。特に外野争いが激化している現状では正当化しがたいぜいたく品だ。フロントは彼を放出するために契約のかなりの部分を負担しなければならないだろうが、忍耐も限界に近づいている」と見ている。状態さえよければ非凡な打撃力を発揮できるが、今や球団の信頼を取り戻すのは難しい。
地元メディア「ボソックス・インジェクション」も「レッドソックスのユニホームを着て最後の時を過ごす選手」として紹介し「彼がプレーオフのロースター入りに値しない理由はあまりに多い。どうフィットするのか想像しにくい」と報じている。

吉田正尚、今季限りで放出も…オフの“退団候補”にレ軍専門サイトが予想「価値が無いと考えられる理由は、あまりにも多い」
吉田の去就は不透明なままだ(C)Getty Images
吉田正尚が所属するレッドソックスは、現地時間9月20日レイズに1-5で敗れたものの、アストロズがブレーブスに2-4で黒星を喫したため、プレーオフ進出が決定した。その一方で、選手の去就にも関心が向けられるシーズン終盤、来季陣容の話題も現地メディアで報じられている。
球団の情報を専門に扱う『BOSOXINJECTION』が20日、「レッドソックス退団が近づいている可能性がある選手」を予想する特集記事を掲載。現在、左太腿を痛め負傷者リスト（IL）入りとなっている吉田をそのうちの1人として候補に挙げている。
ルーキーイヤーの2023年は140試合に出場し、中軸として活躍が注目されたものの、2年目以降は肩や指の故障に悩まされ、フルシーズンでプレー出来ない状況が続いた。またレッドソックスは常に、外野や指名打者で吉田のライバルとなるプレーヤーが多く在籍。背番号7がベンチに座る大きな理由となっている。
同メディアは5年契約を結んでいる吉田が、球団との間でもう1年契約が残っていることから、「（今オフに）トレードで移籍させる場合でも、球団が契約のかなりの部分を負担する可能性が高い。これは、ジョン・ヘンリー・オーナーが簡単に受け入れそうな話ではない」などと主張。
だがその上で、「しかし、33歳のヨシダにロースターの1枠を使う価値が無いと考えられる理由は、あまりにも多い」と訴えている。

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox roster is about to get a bit more crowded as several players are set to return from the injured list before the end of the season. Additionally, even some players who make the cut and play in October might find themselves looking for new homes this winter for a variety of reasons.
One thing the Red Sox have is a solid amount of depth. It's what allowed the club to survive so many injuries and mount a rally after such a horrendous start to the season.
On the flip side, sometimes too much depth is a bad thing. There are only so many roster spots to go around, and at a certain point, Boston needs impact players and not just guys who can hold down the fort in case of emergency.
5 players who are entering their final days as a member of the Red Sox
Masataka Yoshida
We'll start with a controversial one. Getting rid of Masataka Yoshida outright would mean eating $18 million in 2027. Even moving him in a trade would likely result in the Red Sox paying down a good portion of his contract. That doesn't exactly sound like something John Henry would go for.
However, there are just too many reasons why the 33-year-old is no longer worth a roster spot. Injuries have played a major role in Yoshida's Red Sox career. On top of that, it's hard to justify a platoon DH without much power and no defensive ability taking up a roster spot, especially given Boston's outfield logjam. There's a chance he's back from the IL prior to the playoffs starting, but it's hard to see how he fits the postseason roster.
Patrick Sandoval
Patrick Sandoval was a worthwhile dart throw as an injury stash when the Red Sox signed him ahead of the 2025 season. With that said, he's shown that he's not much more than a fifth starter at this point. Boston has an abundance of pitching depth, especially of the left-handed variety, making it a near-certainty that the free-agent-to-be is seeking employment elsewhere this offseason.
Isiah Kiner-Falefa
This is a tough one because, in many ways, Isiah Kiner-Falefa has exceeded expectations this season. The utility infielder is having a career season at the plate and has been a spark plug for Boston. However, does his value hold up as well if his bat falls off more in line with his career averages? There is some intangible value to keeping him around, but it's hard to pony up for a cheerleader when the club has other younger and cheaper options.
Triston Casas
Not technically in a Red Sox uniform due to his litany of injuries, but it's fair to say that Triston Casas' days as a member of the organization are numbered. He can't be counted on to stay healthy. It's unclear what his production would look like after so much time away. Finally, Boston could really do without the headaches. This is a clear non-tender case.
Jahmai Jones
It's starting to become clear why Jahmai Jones never got much of an opportunity to carve out a big league role before 2025. Jones is supposed to mash lefties while playing some outfield and DHing, but for much of the season he's done nothing of the sort. Even his breakout 2025 campaign came over just 150 plate appearances. It's not exactly worth going into arbitration with a player who's failing at executing the one skill he supposedly has.

Red Sox Insert Jahmai Jones into Lineup Against Rays Lefty
The Boston Red Sox placed designated hitter Jahmai Jones in the third spot in the starting lineup on Friday against Tampa Bay Rays left-hander Ian Seymour at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
According to MLB.com, Jones sits in the heart of the order between outfielders Roman Anthony and Wilyer Abreu. Shortstop Trevor Story and first baseman Nick Sogard also feature in the top five positions for Boston.
Left-hander Ranger Suárez gets the start on the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay's Seymour. Seymour enters the contest holding a 9-6 record with a 4.27 ERA and 150 strikeouts on the season, according to official team statistics.
Boston manager Chad Tracy opted to stack the right-handed hitting Jones near the top of the batting order due to ongoing injuries and lack of availability among several key players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Masataka Yoshida, Curtis Mead, and Willson Contreras.
According to MLB Trade Rumors, Boston acquired Jones off waivers on July 14 after the Detroit Tigers designated him for assignment, sending pitching prospect Jojo Ingrassia to Detroit as compensation.
Jones struggled with Detroit this season, batting .137 with a .221 slugging percentage across 105 plate appearances before his release. However, he has turned his season around in Boston, slashing .362/.464/.681 with three home runs and eight RBIs in 56 plate appearances.
Friday marks the 20th time overall this season that Jones has occupied the third spot in a starting lineup, having done so 19 times prior across his stints with Detroit and Boston. In those previous 35 plate appearances in the third spot, he posted a .219 batting average and a .661 OPS.
According to FanGraphs, the platoon splits support Boston's heavy usage of Jones against left-handed pitching. Across 138 plate appearances against lefties this year, Jones has recorded a .223 batting average, a .333 on-base percentage, and a .420 slugging percentage with five home runs, 15 walks, and 14 RBIs.
Conversely, Jones has registered just a .130 average in 23 at-bats against right-handed pitchers, with all five of his home runs this season coming exclusively against left-handers. He previously hit a two-run home run off Seymour during a July 18 matchup at Fenway Park.
Boston enters the three-game series against the American League East-leading Rays with an 83-70 record, holding the second AL Wild Card position and a five-game lead over the Cleveland Guardians. NESN reports Boston's magic number to clinch a postseason berth stands at three with nine games remaining on their schedule.

item.content:encoded:
Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

同メディアは、ポストシーズンのロースターに入れるならコナー・ウォンかミッキー・ガスパー、両捕手のどちらかが押し出される可能性を指摘した。そこで忘れてならないのが、吉田正尚外野手（３３）だ。左太もも裏を痛めて８月１６日（同１７日）に１０日間の負傷者リスト（ＩＬ）へ入ったが、想定より速いペースで復帰へ向かっている。その一方、一部米メディアでは「健康でも１０月は外すべきだ」との厳しい見立ても出ている。
ただ、故障前の吉田は絶好調だった。負傷前の３３試合で打率３割２分１厘、出塁率３割７分７厘、長打率５割５厘。「落選」を当然視できる数字ではなく、短期決戦で、その打力を切り捨てるのは簡単ではない。
ゴンザレスが戻り、吉田まで間に合えば、歓迎すべき戦力回復がそのまま首脳陣の難問に変わる。誰を残し、誰を外すのか。レッドソックスの１０月は、相手との戦いを前に〝最後のイス取りゲーム〟が待っている。

「答えは明確」吉田正尚、復帰してもPS落選か 現地メディアが断言「ロースターから外れるべき」
吉田の置かれている立場は厳しい(C)Getty Images
レッドソックスの吉田正尚は、左太もも裏の張りのため負傷者リスト（IL）入りとなり1か月が経過した。現在もコンディションの回復には至っておらず、今季中の復帰は困難との見方も伝えられている。
また、ポストシーズン進出も視界にとらえるレッドソックスでは、すでに10月の戦力に関する話題も現地メディアを通して伝えられる中で、背番号7には極めて厳しい声が向けられているようだ。
現地時間9月14日、球団の情報を発信する『FANSIDED BOSOXINJECTION』が吉田の起用法を論じる特集記事を配信した。同メディアは、吉田が60日のILには入っていないため、回復の状況次第ではポストシーズンでのメンバー入りもあり得ると指摘する。
その一方で、「たとえヨシダが復帰できたとしても、必ずしもプレーオフのロースターに入れるべきだということにはならない」と主張。今後、26人のロースターを選考する際での“当落線上”の選手と吉田の入れ替えは、「必要無し」と同メディアは訴える。
さらに、ロ―スター外の候補として、ミッキー・ガスパーやニック・ソガードの名前を挙げながらも、「ヨシダのために、ガスパーやソガードをプレーオフのロースターから外すべきではない」と断言。それぞれのパフォーマンスを比較し、吉田については、「87試合に出場して打率.274、出塁率.347、長打率.399、5本塁打。決して悪い数字ではないが、レッドソックスが求める長打力を満たすものとは言い難い」と説明。他にも、「重度のハムストリング負傷から復帰することも考えれば、外野手として戦力になることも期待しにくい」と強調している。

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another.
Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela.
There's a point where push might come to shove, though, and Boston is forced to make a tough choice. Chad Tracy won't rule out Yoshida returning in time for the playoffs, which would lead to some interesting decisions.
"He's [Yoshida] not on the 60-day (injured list). It's just a matter of how does he heal over the next handful of weeks," the interim skipper said.
If the 33-year-old can return in time for October, it could put the likes of Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard in the crosshairs. At which point, the Red Sox will have to make a choice and leave someone unhappy.
Masataka Yoshida shouldn't cost Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard a spot on the Red Sox playoff roster
Just because Yoshida can come back (and that's still up in the air) doesn't mean he should. The NPB veteran has done what he's always done since coming stateside, hit for some average and get on base, but has provided very little in the power department.
Through 87 games, he's hit .274/.347/.399 with five homers, which is nothing to sneeze at, but doesn't really scratch the Red Sox's power itch. On top of that, despite what we saw in the World Baseball Classic, he has little defensive value and will be a nonfactor in the outfield coming off a serious hamstring strain.
Comparatively, Gasper's hot bat better fits what Boston needs. While he might simply be riding the wave rather than emerging as a true offensive force, the switch-hitter has brought the pop with eight dingers in just 187 plate appearances and a .500 slugging percentage, all while providing similar contact and on-base numbers to Yoshida.
Furthermore, he has some value in the field with the ability to fill in behind the plate if needed, as well as play first base. That alone gives him an edge over the DH-only Yoshida.
As for Sogard, his offensive profile is similar to Yoshida's, but his positional versatility is far superior. Depending on Curtis Mead's recovery, Sogard is a valuable insurance policy at second base that should have him over Yoshida in the October pecking order, too.
Craig Breslow's failure to move Jarren Duran before he became a radioactive asset is the real key here. Not only does it represent a missed opportunity for the Red Sox, but it is also the main barrier for Yoshida, given that Boston can't really afford to carry a DH-only player. With that, the choice should be clear. Even if Yoshida is healthy, he needs to sit this October out.

We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
